arXiv:1609.05024v2 [math.AP] 20 Mar 2017

On a cross-diffusion model for multiple species with nonlocal interaction and size exclusion

Judith Berendsen ††thanks: Institut für Numerische und Angewandte Mathematik, Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität (WWU) Münster. Einsteinstr. 62, D 48149 Münster, Germany. e-mail: {judith.berendsen,martin.burger,jan.pietschmann}@wwu.de    Martin Burger    Jan-Frederik Pietschmann
Abstract

The aim of this paper is to study a PDE model for two diffusing species interacting by local size exclusion and global attraction. This leads to a nonlinear degenerate cross-diffusion system, for which we provide a global existence result. The analysis is motivated by the formulation of the system as a formal gradient flow for an appropriate energy functional consisting of entropic terms as well as quadratic nonlocal terms. Key ingredients are entropy dissipation methods as well as the recently developed boundedness by entropy principle. Moreover, we investigate phase separation effects inherent in the cross-diffusion model by an analytical and numerical study of minimizers of the energy functional and their asymptotics to a previously studied case as the diffusivity tends to zero. Finally we briefly discuss coarsening dynamics in the system, which can be observed in numerical results and is motivated by rewriting the PDEs as a system of nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equations.

1 Introduction

Mathematical models with local repulsion and global attraction received strong attention in the last decades, in particular motivated by applications in biology ranging from bacterial chemotaxis (cf. e.g. [17, 25, 47, 55]) to macroscopic motion of animal groups (cf. e.g. [10, 15, 31, 52]) as well as applications in other fields of science (cf. e.g. [62, 45]). The macroscopic modelling of the density evolution leads to partial differential equations with nonlinear diffusion and an additional nonlocal term. The majority of such models can be formulated as metric gradient flows for the density ρ\rho with some energy functional consisting of a local and a nonlocal interaction term

E⁡(ρ)=∫Ωe⁡(ρ)−ρ⁡(K∗ρ)​𝑑x,E(\rho)=\int_{\Omega}e(\rho)-\rho(K*\rho)~dx, (1.1)

where ee is a convex functional, KK a nonnegative interaction kernel, and Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}. Throughout the paper, Ω\Omega may always be unbounded and we will explicitly remark when its boundedness is needed. Various results on the analysis of energy minimizers respectively stationary states (cf. [2, 5, 16, 19, 22, 26, 27, 29, 32, 39, 50, 58, 59]) and the gradient flow dynamics of the form (cf. [6, 9, 8, 16, 28, 30, 36, 65])

∂tρ=∇⋅(M(ρ)∇E′(ρ))\partial_{t}\rho=\nabla\cdot(M(\rho)\nabla E^{\prime}(\rho)) (1.2)

have been achieved in the last years, which led to a good understanding of such models and phenomena.

Much less is known however in the case of multi-species systems, which received most attention only recently (cf. e.g. [1, 14, 13, 20, 44, 54, 57, 60]). With different species, the modelling leads to nonlinear degenerate cross-diffusion systems for the densities of all species, again with some nonlocal terms. The majority of work was concerned with the derivation of models including formal and computational studies, rigorous results are so far mainly available without the nonlocal interaction terms. First rigorous studies of stationary problems (cf. [24, 18, 33]) show interesting phase separation phenomena, whose dynamics seems rather unexplored so far. In this paper we hence study a nonlocal cross-diffusion model for two species called red (density rr) and blue (density bb) for simplicity, which can be derived from a lattice-based microscopic model with size exclusion (cf. [20, 57]):

∂tr\displaystyle\partial_{t}r =∇⋅(ε(1−ρ)∇r+εr∇ρ+r(1−ρ)[∇(c11K∗r−K∗b)+∇V]),\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot(\varepsilon(1-\rho)\nabla r+\varepsilon r\nabla\rho+r(1-\rho)\left[\nabla(c_{11}K\ast r-K\ast b)+\nabla V\right]), (1.3)
∂tb\displaystyle\partial_{t}b =∇⋅(Dε(1−ρ)∇b+Dεb∇ρ+Db(1−ρ)[∇(c22K∗b−K∗r)+∇V]),\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot(D\varepsilon(1-\rho)\nabla b+D\varepsilon b\nabla\rho+Db(1-\rho)\left[\nabla(c_{22}K\ast b-K\ast r)+\nabla V\right]), (1.4)

either on the whole space or in a bounded domain supplemented with no-flux boundary conditions. The positive parameter ε\varepsilon regulates the strength of the diffusion relative to the nonlocal convection terms. Here KK is again the interaction kernel, and the constants ci​i<0c_{ii}<0, i=1,2i=1,2 measure the strength of self-interaction, while the strength of the cross-interaction is scaled to unity (in accordance with the notation of [33]). The time scaling is chosen such that rr has a unit diffusion coefficient, and DD is the potentially different diffusion coefficient of bb. The function ρ\rho is the nonnegative total density

ρ=r+b,\rho=r+b, (1.5)

naturally bounded from above by one. This system (for V≡0V\equiv 0) is a gradient flow for the energy functional

Fε​(r,b)=ε​FE​(r,b)+F0​(r,b).\displaystyle F^{\varepsilon}(r,\,b)=\varepsilon F^{E}(r,b)+F^{0}(r,b). (1.6)

consisting of the nonlocal interaction

F0​(r,b)=∫Ωc11​r​(K∗r)−r⁡(K∗b)−b⁡(K∗r)+c22​b​(K∗b)​𝑑x\displaystyle F^{0}(r,\,b)=\int_{\Omega}c_{11}r(K*r)-r(K*b)-b(K*r)+c_{22}b(K*b)\;dx (1.7)

and the entropy term

FE​(r,b)=∫Ωr​log⁡r+b​log⁡b+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ)​𝑑x.\displaystyle F^{E}(r,\,b)=\int_{\Omega}r\log r+b\log b+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho)\;dx. (1.8)

For Ω\Omega unbounded we need a confining potential VV and the energy is modified to

Eε​(r,b)=Fε​(r,b)+FC​(r,b),FC​(r,b)=∫Ω(r+b)​V​𝑑x.\displaystyle E^{\varepsilon}(r,\,b)=F^{\varepsilon}(r,\,b)+F^{C}(r,\,b),\qquad F^{C}(r,\,b)=\int_{\Omega}(r+b)V\;dx. (1.9)

We shall from now on always use the letter FF to denote the energy without confining potential and EE if the potential is present. This energy is to be considered on the set of bounded densities with given mass

𝒜={(r,b)∈L1(Ω,ℝ+)2:\displaystyle{\cal A}=\{(r,\,b)\in L^{1}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{+})^{2}: (1.10)
∫ℝNrdx=mr,∫ℝNbdx=mb,ρ=r+b≤1 for a.e. x∈Ω},\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}r\;dx=m_{r},\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}b\;dx=m_{b},\rho=r+b\leq 1\text{ for a.e. }x\in\Omega\},

which can be shown to be invariant under the dynamics of (1.3), (1.4). The special case of minimizing F0F^{0} on 𝒜{\cal A} was recently investigated by Cicalese et. al. [33] and it appears obvious that FεF^{\varepsilon} is the natural entropic version and (1.3), (1.4) the natural dynamic model leading to such a minimization problem in the large time asymptotics.

1.1 Connection to Cahn-Hilliard

In order to see the inherent phase separation in (1.3), (1.4) we rewrite it as a system of nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equations. For this sake let KK be nonnegative and integrable with

k=∫ℝNK⁡(x)​𝑑x,k=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}K(x)~dx, (1.11)

which allows to define the nonlocal Laplacian ΔK\Delta_{K} as a negative semidefinite operator via

−ΔK​u=u−1k​K∗u.-\Delta_{K}u=u-\frac{1}{k}K\ast u. (1.12)

Then (1.3), (1.4) becomes

∂tr=∇⋅(kr(1−ρ)∇(c11ΔKr−ΔKb+∂rW(r,b)))\displaystyle\partial_{t}r=\nabla\cdot(kr(1-\rho)\nabla(c_{11}\Delta_{K}r-\Delta_{K}b+\partial_{r}W(r,b))) (1.13)
∂tb=∇⋅(Dkb(1−ρ)∇(c22ΔKb−ΔKr+∂bW(r,b)))\displaystyle\partial_{t}b=\nabla\cdot(Dkb(1-\rho)\nabla(c_{22}\Delta_{K}b-\Delta_{K}r+\partial_{b}W(r,b))) (1.14)

with the multi-well potential

W⁡(r,b)=ε⁡(r​log⁡r+b​log⁡b+(1−ρ)​log⁡(1−ρ))+c112​r2−r​b+c222​b2−c112​r−c222​b.W(r,b)=\varepsilon(r\log r+b\log b+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho))+\frac{c_{11}}{2}r^{2}-rb+\frac{c_{22}}{2}b^{2}-\frac{c_{11}}{2}r-\frac{c_{22}}{2}b. (1.15)

Note that for ε=0\varepsilon=0 the potential has three global minimizers (r,b)(r,b) in the corners of the unit triangle, i.e. (0,1)(0,1), (1,0)(1,0) and (0,0)(0,0). The first two correspond to segregated states and the third one to void, hence those are the main structures to be expected as energy minimizers and in the long time asympotics. For small ε>0\varepsilon>0 the minima are shifted to the interior of the unit triangle and we thus expect less pronounced segregation. For large ε\varepsilon the energy becomes convex and hence we expect mixing instead of segregation. As in other Cahn-Hilliard equations we expect dynamics at two time scales: a short one where clusters - in this case separated in red and blue - appear, and a large one where coarsening dynamics of the clusters appear. In the single species case of the model (1.3), (1.4), e.g. obtained for b≡0b\equiv 0, the coarsening dynamics has been discussed in detail in [21, 34], coarsening rates for a related nonlocal model were derived in [61]. Related work for systems of local Cahn-Hilliard equations (partly with constant mobility) was carried out in [12, 37, 40, 41, 44], supplemented by numerical simulations in [4, 53].

1.2 Organization of the paper

The aim of this work is to analyse the entropic regularization, with parameter ε\varepsilon, of the functional F0F^{0}. We takle this problem from two different perspectives: First we consider the regularized energy from a variational point of view. Second, we study the system of non-local cross-diffusion equations which naturally occur as the gradient flow with respect to this energy.
To this end, we will start by discussing the energy minimization of FεF^{\varepsilon} respectively EεE^{\varepsilon}, we briefly comment on the results in [33] and minor extensions, moreover we verify the Γ\Gamma-convergence of EεE^{\varepsilon} to E0E^{0}. We also prove the existence of minimizers of EεE^{\varepsilon} and their convergence. This is supplemented by a numerical study of the variational problem based on energy minimization via splitting methods. We further show the existence of weak solutions for the transient model (1.3), (1.4), extending the results of [20] to nonlocal interactions and simplifying the line of the proof via appropriate time discretization with regularizing terms in primal and dual (entropy) variables. Moreover, we provide a regularity result in the case of equal diffusivities and verify consistency of the stationary problem with the energy minimization. Finally we study the dynamics in the particularly relevant case of ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 by formal and numerical methods. In the single species case metastable coarsening dynamics of clusters are already studied in detail (cf. [34, 21]) and we obtain similar behaviour in the multi-species setting.

2 Minimizers of the Energy Functionals

We start by stating assumptions on the interaction kernel KK and the potential VV. Furthermore, we define

Definition 2.1 (Coulomb kernel).

The Coulomb kernel on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} is given by

K⁡(x):={−12​|x|for ​N=1,−12​π​log⁡|x|for ​N=2,1(N−2)​ωN​1|x|N−2for ​N≥3,\displaystyle K(x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}-\frac{1}{2}|x|&\text{for }N=1,\\ -\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|&\text{for }N=2,\\ \frac{1}{(N-2)\omega_{N}}\frac{1}{|x|^{N-2}}&\text{for }N\geq 3,\end{array}\right.

where ωN\omega_{N} is the NN-dimensional measure of the unit ball.

While the Coulomb kernel (or Newton-Potential) is a prominent example for our model, we can extend our arguments to a more general class.

Definition 2.2 (Admissible Kernel).

For Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, possibly unbounded, we say that a kernel KK is admissible if the following conditions are satisfied

  • (K1)

    K∈Wl​o​c1,1​(Ω)K\in W^{1,1}_{loc}(\Omega).

  • (K2)

    K is radially symmetric, i.e. K⁡(x)=k⁡(|x|)K(x)=k(|x|) and kk is non-increasing.

  • (K3)

    As x→0x\to 0 and x→∞x\to\infty, KK behaves at most as singular as the Coulomb kernel.

Since VV should act as a confining potential, we impose the following growth condition at infinity.

(V1) Let V∈Wl​o​c1,∞​(ℝN)V\in W^{1,\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) be nonnegative almost everywhere and such that

lim inf|x|→∞V⁡(x)|x|2>0.\liminf_{|x|\to\infty}\frac{V(x)}{|x|^{2}}>0.

2.1 Existence of Minimizers

Let us first summarize the results of Cicalese et. al. concerning the existence of a minimizer of solely the functional F0F^{0} on the whole space ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}.

Theorem 2.3 ([33]).

Let c11,c22≤0c_{11},\,c_{22}\leq 0 and K∈Ll​o​c1​(ℝN)K\in L_{loc}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) and 𝒜{\cal A} as defined in (1.10). Then there exists a minimizer (r0,b0)∈𝒜(r^{0},\,b^{0})\in\mathcal{A} to the functional

F0​(r,b)=∫Ωc11​r​(K∗r)−r⁡(K∗b)−b⁡(K∗r)+c22​b​(K∗b)​𝑑x.\displaystyle F^{0}(r,\,b)=\int_{\Omega}c_{11}r(K*r)-r(K*b)-b(K*r)+c_{22}b(K*b)\,dx.

More precisely let (rn,bn)(r_{n},\,b_{n}) be a minimizing sequence. Then there is a unique sequence of translations (τn)⊂ℝN(\tau_{n})\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} such that up to a subsequence

(rn(⋅−τn),bn(⋅−τn))→(r0,b0)(r_{n}(\cdot-\tau_{n}),b_{n}(\cdot-\tau_{n}))\to(r^{0},\,b^{0})

as n→∞n\to\infty.

Remark 2.4.

Note that due to the translation invariance of F0F^{0}, the results of [33] allow for arbitrary shifts of the minimizers. Adding a confining potential, i.e. replacing F0F^{0} by E0=F0+FCE^{0}=F^{0}+F^{C}, however, does not change their result and removes this technicality.

Next, we extend this existence result to the functionals FεF^{\varepsilon} and EεE^{\varepsilon}, respectively.

Theorem 2.5.

(Existence of Minimizer) Let c11,c22≤0c_{11},\,c_{22}\leq 0 and KK be admissible in the sense of definition 2.2. Then there exists at least one minimizer (r¯,b¯)∈𝒜(\underline{r},\,\underline{b})\in\mathcal{A} to the functional

Eε​(r,b)\displaystyle E^{\varepsilon}(r,b) =ε​FE​(r,b)+F0​(r,b)+FC​(r,b).\displaystyle=\varepsilon F^{E}(r,b)+F^{0}(r,b)+F^{C}(r,b).

More precisely any minimizing sequence (rn,bn)(r_{n},\,b_{n}) converges L1​(Ω)−L^{1}(\Omega)-weakly to a minimizer (r¯,b¯)(\underline{r},\,\underline{b}) of EεE^{\varepsilon} as n→∞n\to\infty.
If, in addition, Ω\Omega is bounded, the same result holds for the functional FεF^{\varepsilon}, i.e. the energy without confining potential.

While the proof of Theorem 2.3 uses Lions’ concentration compactness principle, our approach is based on Dunford-Pettis, making use of the confining potential when Ω\Omega is unbounded.

Theorem 2.6.

(Dunford-Pettis theorem) Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a bounded set in L1​(Ω).L^{1}(\Omega). Then ℱ\mathcal{F} has compact closure in the weak topology σ⁡(L1​(Ω),L∞​(Ω))\sigma(L^{1}(\Omega),L^{\infty}(\Omega)) if and only if ℱ\mathcal{F} is equi-integrable, that is,

(i)\displaystyle(i) ∀ε>0​∃δ>0​ such that ​∫Uf​𝑑x<ε​∀U⊂Ω, measurable with ​|U|<δ,∀f∈ℱ\displaystyle\quad\forall\,\varepsilon>0\;\exists\,\delta>0\text{ such that }\int_{U}f\,dx<\varepsilon\;\forall U\subset\Omega,\text{ measurable with }|U|<\delta,\forall f\in\mathcal{F}
(i​i)\displaystyle(ii) ∀ε>0​∃ω⊂Ω​ measurable with ​|ω|<∞​ such that ​∫Ω∖ωf​𝑑x<ε,∀f∈ℱ.\displaystyle\quad\forall\,\varepsilon>0\;\exists\,\omega\subset\Omega\text{ measurable with }|\omega|<\infty\text{ such that }\int_{\Omega\setminus\omega}f\,dx<\varepsilon,\forall f\in\mathcal{F}.
Remark 2.7.

We carry out the details of the proof for KK being the Coulomb kernel as in Definition 2.1, only. Due to the properties of admissible kernels, the arguments will not change for general KK.

2.2 Structure of Energy Minimizers

The energy minimizers of F0F^{0} on 𝒜{\cal A} could be characterized explicitly in some important cases in [33] using radial symmetrization techniques. In particular they showed that there is no phase separation in the case of cross-attraction being larger than the self-attractions, i.e. c11>−1c_{11}>-1 and c22>−1c_{22}>-1. On the other hand they obtain a strong phase separation result if c11+c22<−2c_{11}+c_{22}<-2 and one of the self-attractions is weak (ci​i>−1c_{ii}>-1). In this case the energy minimizer consists of the strongly attracting species having density one in a ball and the other one having density in a spherical shell around it. The case of strong self-attraction of both species, c11<−1c_{11}<-1, c22<−1c_{22}<-1 was left open in multiple dimension however, noticing that already in dimension one the minimizer is not spherically symmetric. We supplement these results by a generic phase separation result, whose proof closely follows a related result in [18] as well as numerical simulations for N=2N=2 in Section 3:

Proposition 2.8.

Let (r¯,b¯)∈𝒜(\underline{r},\underline{b})\in{\cal A} be a minimizer of F0F^{0} on this admissible set, for KK being a radially strictly decreasing kernel and c11+c22<−2c_{11}+c_{22}<-2. Then the intersection of the supports of r¯\underline{r} and b¯\underline{b} on Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} possibly unbounded has zero Lebesgue measure.

Proof.

Assume by contradiction that there exists an set DD of positive Lebesgue measure and δ0∈(0,12)\delta_{0}\in(0,\frac{1}{2}) such that r¯>δ0\underline{r}>\delta_{0} and b¯>δ0\underline{b}>\delta_{0} on DD. Let dd be the diameter and R<d6R<\frac{d}{6} sufficiently small. 2.3 Convergence as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0

We verify the approximation of E0E^{0} with the entropic terms via a Γ\Gamma-convergence result and the convergence of minimizers. For further studies of the detailed shapes of the minimizers we refer to the numerical examples in Section 5.

Theorem 2.12 (Γ\Gamma-Convergence).

Let Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} be an open and bounded domain. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and for all (r,b)∈𝒜(r,b)\in{\cal A}, the functional

Eε​(r,b)\displaystyle E^{\varepsilon}(r,b)

Γ\Gamma-converges to the functional

E0​(r,b)\displaystyle E^{0}(r,b)

with respect to the weak topology in [L2​(ℝN)]2[L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{N})]^{2}. Furthermore, minimizers (rε,bε)(r^{\varepsilon},b^{\varepsilon}) of EεE^{\varepsilon} converge to minimizers (r0,b0)(r_{0},b_{0}) of E0E^{0} as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Proof.

To prove Γ\Gamma-convergence, we have to check a lim inf⁣−\liminf-inequality and the existence of a recovery sequence, see [11, definition 1.5] for details. To this end consider arbitrary sequences rε,bε∈𝒜r^{\varepsilon},\,b^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{A} that weakly converge to some (r,b)∈𝒜(r,b)\in\mathcal{A} as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. Since on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the functional FEF^{E} is uniformly bounded, is follows that ε​FE\varepsilon F^{E} converges to zero. On the other hand, we know that the interaction terms F0F^{0} are weakly lower semicontinuous and thus we have

E0​(r,b)\displaystyle E^{0}(r,b) ≤lim infε→0Eε​(rε,bε).\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}E^{\varepsilon}(r_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon}). (2.10)

Choosing for every (r,b)∈𝒜(r,b)\in\mathcal{A} the constant sequence as recovery sequence, and using once more the fact that ε​FE\varepsilon F^{E} converges to zero as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 for all (r,b)∈𝒜(r,b)\in\mathcal{A} we have

limε→0Eε​(rε,bε)=E0​(r,b).\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}E^{\varepsilon}(r_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon})=E^{0}(r,b).

This implies the Γ\Gamma-convergence of EεE^{\varepsilon} to E0E^{0}. The fact that the set 𝒜\mathcal{A} is precompact with respect to the weak topology in L2L^{2} trivially implies the coerciveness of EεE^{\varepsilon} and therefore, [11, Theorem 1.21], we have the convergence of minimizers as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 with respect to the weak topology in L2L^{2}. ∎

2.4 Large Scale Structures

Finally we discuss the structures appearing as energy minimizers from a large scale point of view, i.e. we rescale space to a macroscopic variable x~=λ​x\tilde{x}=\lambda x with λ>0\lambda>0 small and assume that the densities can be rewritten as functions r~\tilde{r} and b~\tilde{b} of the new variable x~\tilde{x}. As a consequence of the rescaling we find up to higher order terms in λ\lambda

∫ℝN∫ℝNK⁡(x−y)​r​(x)​b​(y)​𝑑x​𝑑y\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}K(x-y)r(x)b(y)~dx~dy =∫ℝN∫ℝNK⁡(x~−y~λ)​r~​(x~)​b~​(y~)​λ−2​N​𝑑x~​𝑑y~\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}K(\frac{\tilde{x}-\tilde{y}}{\lambda})\tilde{r}(\tilde{x})\tilde{b}(\tilde{y})\lambda^{-2N}~d\tilde{x}~d\tilde{y}
≈λ−N∫ℝNkr~(x~)b~(x~)−Cλ2∇r~(x~)⋅∇b~(x~)dx~,\displaystyle\approx\lambda^{-N}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}k\tilde{r}(\tilde{x})\tilde{b}(\tilde{x})-C\lambda^{2}\nabla\tilde{r}(\tilde{x})\cdot\nabla\tilde{b}(\tilde{x})~d\tilde{x},

with kk defined in (1.11), CC being related to the second moment of KK. With similar approximation of the self-interaction terms the energy λN​F0\lambda^{N}F^{0} equals up to second order

F~λ(r~,b~)=λ2∫ℝN(a112|∇r~|2+a222|∇b~|2+a12∇r~⋅∇b~)dx~+k∫ℝNW(r~,b~)dx~,\tilde{F}^{\lambda}(\tilde{r},\tilde{b})=\lambda^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}(\frac{a_{11}}{2}|\nabla\tilde{r}|^{2}+\frac{a_{22}}{2}|\nabla\tilde{b}|^{2}+a_{12}\nabla\tilde{r}\cdot\nabla\tilde{b})~d\tilde{x}+k\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}W(\tilde{r},\tilde{b})~d\tilde{x},

with WW as in (1.15) with ε=0\varepsilon=0 and

a11=−c11​C,a22=−c22​C,a12=C.a_{11}=-c_{11}C,\quad a_{22}=-c_{22}C,\quad a_{12}=C.

We see that for c11,c22>1c_{11},\,c_{22}>1 the symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrix AA with diagonal entries ai​ia_{ii} und off-diagonal entries a12a_{12} is symmetric. Hence, we may perform a change of variables to (u,v)=A1/2​(r~,b~)(u,v)=A^{1/2}(\tilde{r},\tilde{b}) and obtain the diagonalized problem

Gλ(u,v)=λ22∫ℝN|∇u|2+|∇v|2−kW(A−1/2(u,v))dx~G^{\lambda}(u,v)=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}|\nabla u|^{2}+|\nabla v|^{2}-kW(A^{-1/2}(u,v))~d\tilde{x}

to be minimized on the transformed unit interval

ℬ={(u,v)|A−1/2(u,v)∈𝒜}.{\cal B}=\{(u,v)~|~A^{-1/2}(u,v)\in{\cal A}\}.

The asymptotics of problems of this form has been investigated by Baldo [3], who showed Γ\Gamma-convergence to a multi-phase problem, the limiting functional being a sum of weighted perimeters between the pure phases. Translated to our setting we can conclude that F~λ\tilde{F}^{\lambda} Γ\Gamma-converges to a functional of the form

F~0​(R,B)=dR​B​Per​(∂R∩∂B)+dR​V​Per​(∂R∖∂B)+dB​V​Per​(∂B∖∂R)\tilde{F}^{0}(R,B)=d_{RB}\text{Per}(\partial R\cap\partial B)+d_{RV}\text{Per}(\partial R\setminus\partial B)+d_{BV}\text{Per}(\partial B\setminus\partial R) (2.11)

and weights dR​Bd_{RB}, dR​Vd_{RV}, dB​Vd_{BV} that can be derived from the behaviour of the potential WW, i.e. the values c11c_{11}, c22c_{22}, on the unit triangle. Thus, we see that again that generic energy minimizers are segregated and minimizing structures are determined by the solutions of multiphase versions of the isoperimetric problems.

3 Numerical Study of Minimizers

In this Section we present a numerical algorithm to solve the optimization problem

arg​min(r,b)∈𝒜⁡ε​FE​(r,b)+F0​(r,b)+∫Ω(r+b)​V​dx,\displaystyle\argmin_{(r,b)\in\mathcal{A}}\;\varepsilon F^{E}(r,b)+F^{0}(r,b)+\int_{\Omega}(r+b)V\;dx, (3.1)

We perform our calculation on Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, N=1,2N=1,2, an open and bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. In view of Lemma 2.9, we can then restrict ourselves to the set

𝒜δ:={(r,b)∈\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\delta}:=\{(r,\,b)\in L1​(ℝN,ℝ)2:∫ℝNr​𝑑x=mr,∫ℝNb​𝑑x=mb,\displaystyle L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{N},\mathbb{R})^{2}:\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}r\;dx=m_{r},\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}b\;dx=m_{b}, (3.2)
δ≤r,b,andρ=r+b≤1−δ for a.e. x∈Ω},\displaystyle\delta\leq r,b,\,\mbox{and}\;\rho=r+b\leq 1-\delta\text{ for a.e. }x\in\Omega\}, (3.3)

for some δ>0\delta>0 sufficiently small. Our numerical algorithm is based on a splitting approach. First, we introduce the sets

𝒜M\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{M} :={(r,b)∈L2(Ω)2:∫Ωrdx=mr,∫Ωbdx=mb},\displaystyle:=\{(r,\,b)\in L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}:\int_{\Omega}r\;dx=m_{r},\int_{\Omega}b\;dx=m_{b}\}, (3.4)
𝒜Bδ\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta} :={(r,b)∈L2(Ω)2:δ≤r,b,ρ=r+b≤1−δ for a.e. x∈Ω}.\displaystyle:=\{(r,\,b)\in L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}:\delta\leq r,\,b,\;\rho=r+b\leq 1-\delta\text{ for a.e. }x\in\Omega\}. (3.5)

with the corresponding projections

P𝒜M:L2​(Ω)2→𝒜M,P𝒜M​(r,b)=(r−1|Ω|​(∫Ωr​dx−mr)b−1|Ω|​(∫Ωb​dx−mb))\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}_{M}}:L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}\to\mathcal{A}_{M},\quad P_{\mathcal{A}_{M}}(r,b)=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}r-\frac{1}{|\Omega|}(\int_{\Omega}r\;dx-m_{r})\\ b-\frac{1}{|\Omega|}(\int_{\Omega}b\;dx-m_{b})\end{array}\right)

and

P𝒜Bδ:L2​(Ω)2→𝒜Bδ,P𝒜Bδ​(r,b)=(12​((1−δ)−(b~−r~))12​((1−δ)+(b~−r~)))\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta}}:L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}\to\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta},\quad P_{\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta}}(r,b)=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{1}{2}((1-\delta)-(\tilde{b}-\tilde{r}))\\ \frac{1}{2}((1-\delta)+(\tilde{b}-\tilde{r}))\end{array}\right)

with r~=min⁡(max⁡(r,δ),1−δ)\tilde{r}=\min(\max(r,\delta),1-\delta) and b~=min⁡(max⁡(b,δ),1−δ)\tilde{b}=\min(\max(b,\delta),1-\delta). Obviously, we have 𝒜δ=𝒜Bδ∩𝒜M\mathcal{A}^{\delta}=\mathcal{A}^{\delta}_{B}\cap\mathcal{A}_{M}. Then we consider the problem

arg​min(r1,b1)∈𝒜Bδ,(r2,b2)∈𝒜M\displaystyle\argmin_{(r_{1},b_{1})\in\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta},\,(r_{2},b_{2})\in\mathcal{A}_{M}}\; ε​FE​(r1,b1)+F0​(r2,b2)​𝑑x+∫Ω(r2+b2)​V​𝑑x,\displaystyle\varepsilon F^{E}(r_{1},b_{1})+F^{0}(r_{2},b_{2})\;dx+\int_{\Omega}(r_{2}+b_{2})V\;dx,
such thatr1=r2,b1=b2\displaystyle\mbox{such that}\quad r_{1}=r_{2},\;b_{1}=b_{2}

The corresponding augmented Lagrangian [56, 46], with fixed parameter μ>0\mu>0 is then given by

ℒμ​(r1,b1,r2,b2,λr,λb)=ε​FE​(r1,b1)+F0​(r2,b2)​𝑑x+∫Ω(r2+b2)​V​𝑑x\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(r_{1},b_{1},r_{2},b_{2},\lambda_{r},\lambda_{b})=\varepsilon F^{E}(r_{1},b_{1})+F^{0}(r_{2},b_{2})\;dx+\int_{\Omega}(r_{2}+b_{2})V\;dx
+∫Ωλr(r1−r2)dx+∫Ωλb(b1−b2)dx+μ2(∥r1−r2∥L2​(Ω)2+∥b1−b2∥L2​(Ω)2)\displaystyle\quad+\int_{\Omega}\lambda_{r}(r_{1}-r_{2})\;dx+\int_{\Omega}\lambda_{b}(b_{1}-b_{2})\;dx+\frac{\mu}{2}\left(\|r_{1}-r_{2}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\|b_{1}-b_{2}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\right)

To solve this saddle point problem we use the following ADMM scheme [43]

(r1,b1)n+1\displaystyle(r_{1},b_{1})^{n+1} :=arg​min(r,b)∈𝒜Bδ⁡ℒμ​(r,b,r2n,b2n,λrn,λbn)\displaystyle:=\argmin_{(r,b)\in\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(r,b,r_{2}^{n},b_{2}^{n},\lambda_{r}^{n},\lambda_{b}^{n}) (3.10)
(r2,b2)n+1\displaystyle(r_{2},b_{2})^{n+1} :=arg​min(r,b)∈𝒜M⁡ℒμ​(r1n,b1n,r,b,λrn,λbn)\displaystyle:=\argmin_{(r,b)\in\mathcal{A}_{M}}\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(r_{1}^{n},b_{1}^{n},r,b,\lambda_{r}^{n},\lambda_{b}^{n}) (3.11)
λrn+1\displaystyle\lambda_{r}^{n+1} :=λrn+μ⁡(r1n+1−r2n+1),\displaystyle:=\lambda_{r}^{n}+\mu(r_{1}^{n+1}-r_{2}^{n+1}), (3.12)
λbn+1\displaystyle\lambda_{b}^{n+1} :=λbn+μ⁡(b1n+1−b2n+1)\displaystyle:=\lambda_{b}^{n}+\mu(b_{1}^{n+1}-b_{2}^{n+1}) (3.13)

In order to actually solve the two minimization problems (3.10) and (3.11), we employ a projected gradient method. In fact, for (3.10), the first order optimality condition (of the reduced problem) is given as, [48, Thm 1.48]

(r¯,b¯)∈𝒜Bδ, and ​⟨∇ℒμ​(r¯,b¯,r2n,b2n,λrn,λbn),(r¯b¯)−(rb)⟩∀(r,b)∈𝒜Bδ,\displaystyle(\underline{r},\,\underline{b})\in\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta},\;\text{ and }\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(\underline{r},\underline{b},r_{2}^{n},b_{2}^{n},\lambda_{r}^{n},\lambda_{b}^{n}),\binom{\underline{r}}{\underline{b}}-\binom{r}{b}\rangle\qquad\forall(r,b)\in\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta}, (3.14)

with

∇ℒμ​(r,b,r2n,b2n,λrn,λbn)=(ε⁡[log⁡(r)−log⁡(1−r−b)]+V−λrn−μ⁡(r−r2n)ε⁡[log⁡(b)−log⁡(1−r−b)]+V−λbn−μ⁡(b−b2n)),\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(r,b,r_{2}^{n},b_{2}^{n},\lambda_{r}^{n},\lambda_{b}^{n})=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}\varepsilon[\log(r)-\log(1-r-b)]+V-\lambda_{r}^{n}-\mu(r-r_{2}^{n})\\ \varepsilon[\log(b)-\log(1-r-b)]+V-\lambda_{b}^{n}-\mu(b-b_{2}^{n})\end{array}\right),

which can be shown to be equivalent [48, Lemma 1.12] to

P𝒜Bδ​(∇ℒμ​(r,b,r2n,b2n,λrn,λbn))=0.\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}_{B}^{\delta}}(\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(r,b,r_{2}^{n},b_{2}^{n},\lambda_{r}^{n},\lambda_{b}^{n}))=0.

For (3.11), the corresponding condition gradient is given by

∇ℒμ​(r1n,b1n,r,b,λrn,λbn)=(c11​Vr−Vb+λrn+μ⁡(r−r1n)c22​Vb−Vr+λbn+μ⁡(b−b1n)).\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(r_{1}^{n},b_{1}^{n},r,b,\lambda_{r}^{n},\lambda_{b}^{n})=\left(\begin{array}[]{l}c_{11}V_{r}-V_{b}+\lambda_{r}^{n}+\mu(r-r_{1}^{n})\\ c_{22}V_{b}-V_{r}+\lambda_{b}^{n}+\mu(b-b_{1}^{n})\end{array}\right).

with Vr=K∗rV_{r}=K\ast r and Vb=K∗bV_{b}=K\ast b. To actually solve these problems using a projected steepest descent, we employ a P1 finite element scheme. We only describe the details for the case N=2N=2 (with obvious modifications for N=1N=1). To this end, we approximate Ω\Omega by a polygonal domain Ωh,\Omega_{h}, for which we introduce a conforming triangulation Th={T}T_{h}=\{T\}. As usual, we call h=maxT⁡hTh=\max_{T}h_{T} the mesh size. On Ωh\Omega_{h}, we introduce the space of continuous piecewise linear functions over Ωh\Omega_{h},

Vh={vh∈C(Ωh):vh|T∈P1(T)for all T∈Th}.V_{h}=\{v_{h}\in C(\Omega_{h}):v_{h}|_{T}\in P_{1}(T)\quad\text{for all }T\in T_{h}\}.

Note that by construction Vh⊂H1​(Ωh)V_{h}\subset H^{1}(\Omega_{h}). Since we restricted ourselves to KK being the Coulomb-Kernel, calculating the convolution u=K∗ru=K\ast r is equivalent to solving the problem

−Δ​u\displaystyle-\Delta u =r, in ​Ω\displaystyle=r,\;\text{ in }\Omega (3.19)
u\displaystyle u =0, on ​∂Ω.\displaystyle=0,\;\text{ on }\partial\Omega. (3.20)

For all computations, we use a P1 finite element approximation. The use of first order finite elements has the important merit that the coefficient vector containts the node values and therefore, we can directly apply the projection (3) on the box constraints 𝒜B{\cal A}_{B} (for (3) we have to employ the mass matrix in order to evaluate the integral). For extensions to higher order finite elements see [63]. All examples are implemented in MATLAB.
All one-dimensional calculation are done on the domain Ω1=[−1,1]\Omega_{1}=[-1,1] while in two dimensions we used the circle with radius r=2r=2, i.e. Ω2=B2​(0)\Omega_{2}=B_{2}(0).

3.1 Examples in Spatial Dimension One

We start by numerically verifying the results of Cicalese et. al. [33]. The potential is given by

V⁡(x)={(x−0.5)2x>0.5,(x+0.5)2x<0.5,0otherwise.\displaystyle V(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}(x-0.5)^{2}&x>0.5,\\ (x+0.5)^{2}&x<0.5,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{array}\right.

We initialize both rr and bb with random values in the interval [0,0.49][0,0.49] which ensures ρ≤0.98<1\rho\leq 0.98<1. We use the ADMM scheme described above with step size τ=0.01\tau=0.01 and take 10001000 points to discretize space for the projected gradient iterations. We are able to numerically verify the different cases as depicted in [33, Figure 2] for the Coulomb kernel. The results are shown in Figure 1.

While all these examples are symmetric with respect to the origin, we can also obtain the asymmetric cases which appear for either c11=−1c_{11}=-1 and c22<−1c_{22}<-1 and c11<−1c_{11}<-1 or c22=−1c_{22}=-1, see Figure 2. To break the symmetry, we multiplied the random initial data of rr by the positive function 0.3​x+10.3x+1. For the case (−1,−2)(-1,-2), left picture of Figure 2, we obtain one density surrounded by the other and taking the same initial conditions but values (−2,1)(-2,1), we see that the support of the minimizers separate. This, for N=2N=2, corresponds to the situation where the smaller ball touches the boundary of the larger one, see again [33, Figure 2]. Finally, again for (−2,1)(-2,1) but the random initial data for bb multiplied by x+1x+1, we obtain a picture anti-symmetric to the first one, shown on the right. Since all initial guesses have the same mass, this also illustrates the non-uniqueness of minimizers.

Next, we solve the minimization problem (3.1) for values ε=0.01, 0.05, 0.1\varepsilon=0.01,\,0.05,\,0.1. In Figure 3, we compare the corresponding minimizers to the case ε=0\varepsilon=0 with the choice c11=−1c_{11}=-1 and c22=−1.5c_{22}=-1.5. As expected, for small ε\varepsilon, the entropic part of the functional causes a smoothing of the minimizers. For larger ε\varepsilon, the energy becomes convex and we observe mixing without phase seperation as discussed in the introduction. This is also illustrated in Figure 3, where the integral of r​brb over Ω\Omega is evaluated for different values of ε\varepsilon. For small values, a linear increase is observed while for large values, the overlap becomes very large and the integral cannot serve as an indicator for the overlap anymore.

3.2 Examples in Spatial Dimension Two

Next, we use our algorithm to solve the minimization problem in two spatial dimensions. Again, we first verify that we can reproduce the results of [33]. This is shown in Figure 4. We do not show the simulations for different ε\varepsilon since the results are very similar to the ones in one spatial dimension. The only difference is that we are not able to produce an asymmetric situation. For example, in Figure 4, right picture, we have the case c11=−1,c22=−3c_{11}=-1,\,c_{22}=-3 with mr=0.2m_{r}=0.2, mb=0.4m_{b}=0.4 and asymmetric initial data, yet we obtain a completely symmetric result. The same holds true for simulations with both c11c_{11} and c22c_{22} smaller than one.

More interesting is again the case

c11<−1,c22<−1.\displaystyle c_{11}<-1,\;c_{22}<-1.

In [33], an explicit characterization of minimizers in this case is only possible in one spatial dimension. It is, however, known that for N>1N>1, minimizers are characteristic functions of sets. By performing simulations, we confirm this results and are also able to characterize minimizers more precisely. In fact, for c11=c22=−2c_{11}=c_{22}=-2 and mr=mb=1/3m_{r}=m_{b}=1/3, we see that the minimizers are two half balls, Figure 5 (left). Changing the mass of one species, we see that the interface between then changes from a straight line as in the previous case to a curved structure, Figure 5 (second from left). Varying also the constants c11c_{11} and c22c_{22}, as well as the masses, leads to similar results, see Figure 5 (third from left and right picture).

It is instructive to reinterpret the last results in view of (2.11). In the second column of Figure 4 we find the situation dR​V>dR​B>dB​Vd_{RV}>d_{RB}>d_{BV}. Hence it is energetically favourable to avoid the interface between red and void, and put the largest interface between blue and void, which leads to an isoperimetric problem for the overall density. The partioning inside is simply obtained by a local isoperimetric problem for the red phase. The third column can be equally explained with the setting dB​V>dR​B>dR​Vd_{BV}>d_{RB}>d_{RV}. The situation in Figure 5 is more subtle. Here dR​Vd_{RV} and dB​Vd_{BV} are expected to be lower than dB​Vd_{BV} but the difference seems not large enough that a separation into two disjoint structures is favourable. On the other hand for dR​Bd_{RB} large it is not favourable to create a ring as in Figure 4, but there is a local partitioning inside the ball leading to a smaller perimeter of the interface. We mention that numerical simulations with very large absolute values of the ci​ic_{ii} yield similar results, hence it is not clear whether the case of dR​Bd_{RB} so large that it is favourable to create two separate structures for red and blue can be obtained as an asymptotic from our model.

4 Transient Model

As described in the introduction, minimizers of (1.6) are closely related to solutions of systems of nonlinear cross-diffusion partial differential equations [20]. In fact, introducing the nonlinear diagonal mobility tensor 𝐌⁡(r,b){\bf M}(r,b) given by

𝐌⁡(r,b)=(r⁡(1−ρ)00D​b​(1−ρ)){\bf M}(r,b)=\left(\begin{matrix}r(1-\rho)&0\\ 0&Db(1-\rho)\end{matrix}\right)

we can introduce the following formal gradient flow with respect to EεE^{\varepsilon}

∂t(rb)=∇⋅(𝐌⁡(r,b):∇(∂rEε​(r,b)∂bEε​(r,b))).\partial_{t}\left(\begin{array}[]{l}r\\ b\end{array}\right)=\nabla\cdot\left({\bf M}(r,b){\bf:}\nabla\left(\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{r}E^{\varepsilon}(r,b)\\ \partial_{b}E^{\varepsilon}(r,b)\end{array}\right)\right). (4.1)

Inserting the definition (1.9) of EεE^{\varepsilon}, we obtain (1.3)-(1.4). This system is set on a domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. If Ω\Omega is bounded, we impose the following no-flux boundary conditions

n⋅((1−ρ)∇r+r∇ρ+r(1−ρ)[∇(c11K∗r−K∗b)+∇V])\displaystyle n\cdot((1-\rho)\nabla r+r\nabla\rho+r(1-\rho)\left[\nabla(c_{11}K\ast r-K\ast b)+\nabla V\right]) =0,\displaystyle=0, (4.2)
n⋅((1−ρ)∇b+b∇ρ+b(1−ρ)[∇(c22K∗b−K∗r)+∇V])\displaystyle n\cdot((1-\rho)\nabla b+b\nabla\rho+b(1-\rho)\left[\nabla(c_{22}K\ast b-K\ast r)+\nabla V\right]) =0,\displaystyle=0,

on ∂Ω×(0,T)\partial\Omega\times(0,T). This system is further supplemented by initial values

r⁡(⋅,0)=r0,b⁡(⋅,0)=b0​ in ​Ω.r(\cdot,0)=r_{0},\quad b(\cdot,0)=b_{0}\text{ in }\Omega. (4.3)

Using the functional ε​FE+FC\varepsilon F^{E}+F^{C}, we introduce entropy variables, given as the first derivative with respect to rr and bb

u:=∂r(ε​FE+FC)\displaystyle u:=\partial_{r}(\varepsilon F^{E}+F^{C}) =ε⁡(log⁡r−log⁡(1−ρ))+V,\displaystyle=\varepsilon(\log r-\log(1-\rho))+V, (4.4)
v:=∂b(ε​FE+FC)\displaystyle v:=\partial_{b}(\varepsilon F^{E}+F^{C}) =ε⁡(log⁡b−log⁡(1−ρ))+V.\displaystyle=\varepsilon(\log b-\log(1-\rho))+V. (4.5)

Inverting these relations yields

r=eu−Vε1+eu−Vε+ev−Vε,b=ev−Vε1+eu−Vε+ev−Vε.\displaystyle r=\frac{e^{\frac{u-V}{\varepsilon}}}{1+e^{\frac{u-V}{\varepsilon}}+e^{\frac{v-V}{\varepsilon}}},\quad b=\frac{e^{\frac{v-V}{\varepsilon}}}{1+e^{\frac{u-V}{\varepsilon}}+e^{\frac{v-V}{\varepsilon}}}. (4.6)

4.1 Existence of weak solutions

For further use we define the set ℳ\mathcal{M}

ℳ={(r,b)∈[L2(Ω),ℝ+]2:0<r,b;r+b=ρ<1 a.e.}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\{(r,\,b)\in[L^{2}(\Omega),\mathbb{R}^{+}]^{2}:0<r,\,b;\,r+b=\rho<1\text{ a.e.}\}.

Global existence is guaranteed by the following theorem

Theorem 4.1.

Let T>0T>0, ε>0\varepsilon>0 and D>0D>0. Consider the following partial differential equations on an open and bounded Lipschitz domain Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}

∂tr\displaystyle\partial_{t}r =∇⋅(ε[(1−ρ)∇r+r∇ρ]+r(1−ρ)∇V+r(1−ρ)∇(c11K∗r−K∗b))\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot(\varepsilon[(1-\rho)\nabla r+r\nabla\rho]+r(1-\rho)\nabla V+r(1-\rho)\nabla(c_{11}K\ast r-K\ast b)) (4.7)
∂tb\displaystyle\partial_{t}b =∇⋅(εD[(1−ρ)∇b+b∇ρ]+b(1−ρ)∇V+Db(1−ρ)∇(c22K∗b−K∗r))\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot(\varepsilon D[(1-\rho)\nabla b+b\nabla\rho]+b(1-\rho)\nabla V+Db(1-\rho)\nabla(c_{22}K\ast b-K\ast r)) (4.8)

for VV satisfying (V1), ci​j≤0c_{ij}\leq 0 for i,j∈{1,2}i,\,j\in\{1,2\} and KK as in definition (2.2). The system is equipped with initial conditions

r⁡(⋅, 0)=r0andb⁡(⋅, 0)=b0\displaystyle r(\cdot,\,0)=r_{0}\quad\text{and}\quad b(\cdot,\,0)=b_{0}

with (r0,b0)∈ℳ(r_{0},b_{0})\in\mathcal{M} and no flux boundary conditions (4.2). Then there exists a weak solution (r,b)(r,\,b) in

W=(L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))∩H1​((0,T),H−1​(Ω)))2W=(L^{2}((0,T),\,L^{2}(\Omega))\cap H^{1}((0,\,T),\,H^{-1}(\Omega)))^{2}

We remark that the proof without non-local interactions is given in [20, Theorem 4.1], yet using a different approximation technique. Here, we use a semi-discretization in time that has also been used in [23], but applied to a different, anisotropic system.

Proof.

Without loss of generality we choose D=1D=1 in the proof and furthermore denote by CC a generic constant whose value can change from line to line. For different D>0D>0, some constants change yet the arguments remain the same. We prove the theorem in three steps: First we obtain an a priori bound based on the entropy dissipation, second we apply a time discretization and use a fixed point argument to ensure existence of weak solutions for every time step. Finally, we finish the proof passing to continuous time.

ℱ:ℳ→ℳ,(r~,b~)→(r,b)=D​E−1​(u,v)\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{M},(\tilde{r},\,\tilde{b})\to(r,\,b)=DE^{-1}(u,\,v)

‖r‖L2​(Ω)≤‖r‖L∞​(Ω)​|Ω|=|Ω|<∞\|r\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\leq\|r\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}|\Omega|=|\Omega|<\infty

and the analogue for the second component b.b. It remains to establish compactness of ℱ\mathcal{F}. Finally, the fact that the mapping (4.6) is differentiable and thus Lipschitz continuous, we conclude the continuity of the whole operator ℱ\mathcal{F}. In order to pass to the limit τ→0\tau\to 0 and to show the convergence rτ→rr_{\tau}\to r and bτ→bb_{\tau}\to b we need the following two lemmas.

Lemma 4.2.

The following estimates hold for a constant C~∈ℝ+\tilde{C}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and rτ,bτ∈L∞​(Ω)r_{\tau},\,b_{\tau}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega)

‖1−ρτ‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))+‖ρτ‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))\displaystyle\|\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}\|_{L^{2}((0,T),\,H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|\rho_{\tau}\|_{L^{2}((0,T),\,H^{1}(\Omega))} ≤C~\displaystyle\leq\tilde{C} (4.63)
τ​(‖uτ‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))+‖vτ‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)))\displaystyle\sqrt{\tau}(\|u_{\tau}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|v_{\tau}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}) ≤C~\displaystyle\leq\tilde{C} (4.64)
Lemma 4.3.

The discrete time derivatives of rτr_{\tau} and bτb_{\tau} are uniformly bounded

1τ​‖rτ−στ​rτ‖L2​((0,T),H−1​(Ω))+1τ​‖bτ−στ​bτ‖L2​((0,T),H−1​(Ω))≤C.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau}\|r_{\tau}-\sigma_{\tau}r_{\tau}\|_{L^{2}((0,T),\,H^{-1}(\Omega))}+\frac{1}{\tau}\|b_{\tau}-\sigma_{\tau}b_{\tau}\|_{L^{2}((0,T),\,H^{-1}(\Omega))}\leq C. (4.65)

The first lemma is a direct consequence of the discrete in time entropy inequality (4.1), see [57, 23] for details. The second results from using the estimates of the first one in the weak formulation (4.1). Now we apply a special version of the Aubins-Lions lemma specifically designed for piecewise constant interpolations, cf. [35, Theorem 1]. Using the Gelfand triple H1​(Ω)↪L2​(Ω)↪H−1​(Ω),H^{1}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow H^{-1}(\Omega), this theorem implies that (4.65) together with the boundedness of ρτ\rho_{\tau} in L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)) is sufficient to obtain a strongly converging subsequence such that (without relabeling)

ρτ→ρ​ in ​L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))​ as ​τ→0.\displaystyle\rho_{\tau}\to\rho\text{ in }L^{2}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega))\text{ as }\tau\to 0.

This implies

1−ρτ→1−ρinL4​((0,T),L4​(Ω)).\displaystyle\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}\to\sqrt{1-\rho}\quad\text{in}\quad L^{4}((0,T),\,L^{4}(\Omega)).

But since the space L4​((0,T),L4​(Ω))L^{4}((0,T),\,L^{4}(\Omega)) embeds continuously in L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω)),L^{2}((0,T),\,L^{2}(\Omega)), the function 1−ρτ\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}} must also converge strongly to 1−ρ\sqrt{1-\rho} in L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))L^{2}((0,T),\,L^{2}(\Omega)). Note that (4.64) immediately implies

τ​uτ,τ​vτ→0​ as ​τ→0​ strongly in ​L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)),\displaystyle\tau u_{\tau},\,\tau v_{\tau}\to 0\text{ as }\tau\to 0\text{ strongly in }L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)),
τ∇uτ,τ∇vτ→0 as τ→0 strongly in L2((0,T);[L2(Ω)]N).\displaystyle\tau\nabla u_{\tau},\,\tau\nabla v_{\tau}\to 0\text{ as }\tau\to 0\text{ strongly in }L^{2}((0,T);[L^{2}(\Omega)]^{N}).

Finally, since rτ,bτr_{\tau},\,b_{\tau} are uniformly bounded in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega), we know that there exist subsequences such that

rτ⇀∗r,bτ⇀∗b in L∞((0,T);L∞(Ω)).\displaystyle r_{\tau}\rightharpoonup^{*}r,\;b_{\tau}\rightharpoonup^{*}b\quad\text{ in }L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{\infty}(\Omega)). (4.66)

In order to be able to pass to the limit in (4.1), we rewrite

(1−ρτ)∇rτ+rτ∇ρτ=1−ρτ∇(1−ρτrτ)−31−ρτrτ∇1−ρτ\displaystyle(1-\rho_{\tau})\nabla r_{\tau}+r_{\tau}\nabla\rho_{\tau}=\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}\nabla(\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}r_{\tau})-3\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}r_{\tau}\nabla\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}

The first term on the right hand side can be dealt with by further expanding the term ∇(1−ρτ​rτ)\nabla(\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}r_{\tau}), the fact that 1−ρτ\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}} converges strongly, using the bounds (4.62) and the fact (4.66). For the second term, one has to prove strong convergence of 1−ρτ​rτ,\sqrt{1-\rho_{\tau}}r_{\tau}, which can be done either by using the Kolmogorov-Riesz theorem, see [20] or again a generalized Aubins-Lions lemma, see [64]. Note that this strong convergence also allows us to identify the corresponding, weakly converging gradient. ∎

As a next step, we extend the previous result to the case Ω=ℝN\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{N}. The crucial ingredient will be the entropy inequality, which also holds on the whole space. We have

Theorem 4.4.

Let T>0T>0, ε>0\varepsilon>0, Ω=ℝN\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{N} and the assumptions on VV, KK and the constants c11c_{11} and c22c_{22} as in Theorem 2.5. Then, the system (4.7)–(4.8), with initial conditions

r⁡(⋅, 0)=r0andb⁡(⋅, 0)=b0\displaystyle r(\cdot,\,0)=r_{0}\quad\text{and}\quad b(\cdot,\,0)=b_{0}

with (r0,b0)∈ℳ(r_{0},b_{0})\in\mathcal{M} and the additional requirement that the second moment of both r0r_{0} and b0b_{0} are bounded. Then there exists a weak solution (r,b)(r,\,b) in

W=(L2​((0,T),L2​(ℝN))∩H1​((0,T),H−1​(ℝN)))2\displaystyle W=(L^{2}((0,T),\,L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{N}))\cap H^{1}((0,\,T),\,H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{N})))^{2}

such that

ρ,1−ρ​r,1−ρ​b∈L2​((0,T),H1​(ℝN)),\displaystyle\rho,\,\sqrt{1-\rho}r,\,\sqrt{1-\rho}b\in L^{2}((0,\,T),\,H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{N})),

and furthermore 0≤r,b0\leq r,\,b and ρ≤1\rho\leq 1 almost everywhere.

Proof.

The proof is based on the same a priori estimates as in the bounded domain case and thus we only sketch the additional arguments. Indeed, the main ingredient is the entropy inequality, (4.11) which, due to the uniform L1∩L∞L^{1}\cap L^{\infty}-bounds on rr and bb also holds on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}. This in particular implies the second moment bound on rr and bb which in turn yields the compactness of the embedding from H1​(ℝN)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) to L2​(ℝN)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{N}). Indeed, taking a sequence un∈H1​(ℝN)u_{n}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) we have, for some u∈L2u\in L^{2} and fixed R>0R>0 that

∫ℝN(u−un)2​𝑑x=∫BR​(0)(u−un)2​𝑑x+∫ℝN∖BR​(0)(u−un)2​𝑑x.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}(u-u_{n})^{2}\;dx=\int_{B_{R}(0)}(u-u_{n})^{2}\;dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}\setminus B_{R}(0)}(u-u_{n})^{2}\;dx.

Using the L∞L^{\infty}-bound on unu_{n} and uu, we can estimate the second term on the right hand side and obtain

∫ℝN(u−un)2​𝑑x≤∫BR​(0)(u−un)2​𝑑x+1R2|u−un|∫ℝN∖BR​(0)L∞​(ℝN)⁡|x|2​(u−un)​𝑑x.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}(u-u_{n})^{2}\;dx\leq\int_{B_{R}(0)}(u-u_{n})^{2}\;dx+\frac{1}{R^{2}}\|u-u_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N})}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}\setminus B_{R}(0)}|x|^{2}(u-u_{n})\;dx.

Taking the lim supn→∞\limsup_{n\to\infty}, we see that the first term on the right hand side vanishes due to the compactness of H1​(BR​(0))↪L2​(BR​(0))H^{1}(B_{R}(0))\hookrightarrow L^{2}(B_{R}(0)) for fixed RR. Taking, in a second step the limit R→∞R\to\infty yields the assertion.
Now we generate a sequence of approximate solutions rnr_{n} and bnb_{n} by solving the problem

∫0T∫Bn​(0)(∂trn∂tbn)⋅(Φ1Φ2)​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫0T∫Bn​(0)((1−ρn)∇rn+rn∇ρn(1−ρn)∇bn+bn∇ρn)⋅(∇Φ1∇Φ2)​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{B_{n}(0)}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\partial_{t}r_{n}\\ \partial_{t}b_{n}\end{array}\right)\cdot\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\Phi_{1}\\ \Phi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right)\,dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{B_{n}(0)}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}(1-\rho_{n})\nabla r_{n}+r_{n}\nabla\rho_{n}\\ (1-\rho_{n})\nabla b_{n}+b_{n}\nabla\rho_{n}\end{array}\right)\cdot\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\nabla\Phi_{1}\\ \nabla\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right)\,dxdt
+∫0T∫Bn​(0)H(rτ,bτ)(∇Φ1∇Φ2)dxdt=0,\displaystyle\quad+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{B_{n}(0)}H(r_{\tau},\,b_{\tau})\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\nabla\Phi_{1}\\ \nabla\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right)\,dxdt=0,

where we use restrictions of r0r_{0} and b0b_{0} to Bn​(0)B_{n}(0) as initital conditions. Due to the two ingredients, namely entropy inequality and compactness, we can pass to the limit exactly the same way as we did for time discretization in the proof of the previous theorem. The bounds of the right hand side of the weak formulation (4.1), again together with the second moment bound, then also yield the H−1​(ℝN)H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{N})-bounds for the time derivatives. ∎

For D=1D=1, we have the following regularity result for ρ\rho which may serve as a first step in proving uniqueness of solutions via a fixed point argument in that case.

Proposition 4.5 (Regularity of ρ\rho for D=1D=1).

Assume that the diffusion coefficient DD is one, and let (r,b)(r,b) be a weak solution to (4.7)–(4.8). Then, on a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω\Omega, there are positive constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} such that the sum r+b=ρr+b=\rho satisfies the following a priori estimate

‖ρ‖L∞​(0,T,W1,p​(Ω))≤C1+C2​‖ρ0‖W1,p​(Ω),\displaystyle\|\rho\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;W^{1,p}(\Omega))}\leq C_{1}+C_{2}\|\rho_{0}\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)},

for all 2≤p<∞.2\leq p<\infty.

Proof.

For D=1D=1, we can add equations (4.7) and (4.8) to obtain an equation for ρ\rho given as

∂tρ−εΔρ=−∇⋅h\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho-\varepsilon\Delta\rho=-\nabla\cdot h (4.77)

with

h:=r(1−ρ)(c11∇K∗r−K∗b)+b(1−ρ)(c22∇K∗b−K∗r).\displaystyle h:=r(1-\rho)(c_{11}\nabla K\ast r-K\ast b)+b(1-\rho)(c_{22}\nabla K\ast b-K\ast r).

and initial datum

ρ⁡(⋅,0)=ρ0​ in ​W1,p​(Ω).\displaystyle\rho(\cdot,0)=\rho_{0}\text{ in }W^{1,p}(\Omega).

Using the regularity of rr and bb as well as the properties of KK, we can estimate hh as follows

‖h⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)\displaystyle\|h(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} ≤14​‖∇K‖L1​(Ω)​[(c11−1)​‖r⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+(c22−1)​‖b⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)]=C\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4}\|\nabla K\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}\left[(c_{11}-1)\|r(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+(c_{22}-1)\|b(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\right]=C

Since the constant on the right hand side does not depend on tt we can take the supremum over all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and conclude that h∈L∞​((0,T),L∞​(Ω))h\in L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{\infty}(\Omega)). Thus applying the LpL^{p} theory for linear parabolic equation, see e.g. [51, Chapter VII], yields the assertion. ∎

Remark 4.6 (Minimizers as stationary solutions).

By remark 2.11 we know that minimizers of the energy EεE^{\varepsilon} are in fact in the space [W1,∞​(Ω)]2[W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)]^{2}. Therefore they can be inserted in the weak formulation of the stationary equation and are thus also stationary solutions of the PDE system (4.7)–(4.8) with no flux boundary conditions.

5 Numerical Simulations

This Section deals with a numerical algorithm to solve the the PDE system (4.7)–(4.8) supplemented with no flux boundary conditions. We use the same P11 finite element method as described in (3). To discretize in time, we use the following implicit-explicit scheme: Given inital values r0,b0∈Vhr^{0},\,b^{0}\in V_{h} and denoting the current iterates by rn,bnr^{n},b^{n} (with ρn=rn+bn\rho^{n}=r^{n}+b^{n}), we obtain new iterates rn+1,bn+1r^{n+1},\,b^{n+1} by solving the linear system

∫Ωrn+1​φ​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}r^{n+1}\varphi\;dx =∫Ωrnφdx+τ∫Ωε[(1−bn)∇rn+1+rn∇bn+1]⋅∇φdx\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}r^{n}\varphi\;dx+\tau\int_{\Omega}\varepsilon\left[(1-b^{n})\nabla r^{n+1}+r^{n}\nabla b^{n+1}\right]\cdot\nabla\varphi\;dx
+(1−ρn)∇(c11K∗rn−K∗bn+V)⋅∇φdx\displaystyle+(1-\rho^{n})\nabla(c_{11}K\ast r^{n}-K\ast b^{n}+V)\cdot\nabla\varphi\;dx
∫Ωbn+1​φ​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}b^{n+1}\varphi\;dx =∫Ωbnφdx+τ∫Ωε[(1−rn)∇bn+1+bn∇rn+1]⋅∇φdx\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}b^{n}\varphi\;dx+\tau\int_{\Omega}\varepsilon\left[(1-r^{n})\nabla b^{n+1}+b^{n}\nabla r^{n+1}\right]\cdot\nabla\varphi\;dx
+(1−ρn)∇(c22K∗bn−K∗rn+V)⋅∇φdx.\displaystyle+(1-\rho^{n})\nabla(c_{22}K\ast b^{n}-K\ast r^{n}+V)\cdot\nabla\varphi\;dx.

with time step size τ>0\tau>0 given. Again, we use MATLAB for the implementation, both in one and two spatial dimensions.

5.1 Examples in one spatial dimensions

For all one-dimensional examples, we use the same potential VV as in Section 3, defined in (3.1) Furthermore, to decide when we reached a stationary state, we consider the relative L2L^{2}-error between two iterates, i.e

errL2:=‖rn−rn−1‖L2​(Vh)+‖bn−bn−1‖L2​(Vh)\displaystyle\mathrm{err}_{L^{2}}:=\|r^{n}-r^{n-1}\|_{L^{2}(V_{h})}+\|b^{n}-b^{n-1}\|_{L^{2}(V_{h})}

and stop the iteration as soon as errL2<1​e−12\mathrm{err}_{L^{2}}<1e-12. We start by comparing the solutions for different values of ε\varepsilon to that of the ADMM scheme. As initial values we take

r=b=13​Hγ​(12−|x|), with ​γ=0.001,\displaystyle r=b=\frac{1}{3}H_{\gamma}\left(\frac{1}{2}-|x|\right),\text{ with }\gamma=0.001, (5.1)

where HγH^{\gamma} is the following approximation of the Heaviside function

Hγ​(r)=1π​(π2+atan⁡(rγ)),γ>0.\displaystyle H_{\gamma}(r)=\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\mathrm{atan}(\frac{r}{\gamma})\right),\quad\gamma>0. (5.2)

The results are visualized in Figure 6 (left). In the top right picture the number of iterations until the error criterion is met are shown. On the bottom right, we plot, for a fixed time t=19t=19 (and thus a fixed number of iterations), the relative error that is achieved for different values of ε\varepsilon. As expected, both plots confirm that the dynamics become slower as ε\varepsilon becomes smaller - see the discussion about the relationship to systems of Cahn-Hilliards equations in the introduction.

As a next step, we examine the dynamical behaviour of solutions. To this end we consider a situation where initially, two compactly supported bumbs of both rr and bb are centered at x=±0.6x=\pm 0.6 in the domain, see Figure 7. All subsequent simulations are done for ε=0.0002\varepsilon=0.0002 and τ=0.0005\tau=0.0005. First we examined the case c11=−2c_{11}=-2 and c22=−0.5c_{22}=-0.5 in which we observe unmixing of the two species first, before the two populations meet, see Figure 8. In the case c11=−1c_{11}=-1 and c22=−0.5c_{22}=-0.5, we observe only a partial unmixing until the two densities meet, see Figure 9.

5.2 Examples in two spatial dimensions

In two dimensions, we only present one example showing that for large tt, the solutions of the system seem in fact to converge to the minimizers obtained by the ADMM scheme. To this end, we chose again the case c11=−1c_{11}=-1 and c22=−1/2c_{22}=-1/2 and ε=0.02\varepsilon=0.02 and used the solution of the PDE at time t=650t=650. The results are shown in figure 10. Note that our present results only ensure the existence of solution for arbitrary large yet finite time. However, we expect that these can be extended to the case t→∞t\to\infty and that we can in fact show convergence to stationary solutions by means of relative entropy methods.

6 Outlook: Coarsening Dynamics

In the following we further investigate the coarsening dynamics of the system (1.3), (1.4) as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Let us first of all discuss the case ε=0\varepsilon=0, which is characterized by a very large set of stationary solutions. Indeed, every pair (r¯,b¯)(\overline{r},\overline{b}) with

r¯​(1−r¯−b¯)=b¯​(1−r¯−b¯)=0\overline{r}(1-\overline{r}-\overline{b})=\overline{b}(1-\overline{r}-\overline{b})=0 (6.1)

is a stationary solution, but not necessarily stable under the dynamics. In the case for a single species, stability was characterized from an entropy condition in [21], noticing that the model for ε=0\varepsilon=0 consists of nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with nonlocal terms. A generalization of the entropy condition to the system case seems out of reach, hence we revisit the single species case (b=0b=0 in our notation) and rederive the stability condition from an optimization argument. Intuitively a stationary state is stable if it is a local minimizer of the energy, and using a Lagrange multiplier λr\lambda_{r} for the mass constraint we easily arrive at the conditions

c11​K∗r⁡(x)+λr≥0\displaystyle c_{11}K*r(x)+\lambda_{r}\geq 0 if ​r​(x)=0\displaystyle\quad\text{if }r(x)=0
c11​K∗r⁡(x)+λr≤0\displaystyle c_{11}K*r(x)+\lambda_{r}\leq 0 if ​r​(x)=1.\displaystyle\quad\text{if }r(x)=1.

Thus, at an interface between a region with r=1r=1 inside and r=0r=0 outside the normal derivative of S=c11​K∗rS=c_{11}K*r is nonpositive, which is exactly the entropy condition derived in [34, 21].

In the system case we find by analogous arguments with Lagrange parameters λr\lambda_{r} and λb\lambda_{b} for the masses

c11​K∗r⁡(x)−K∗b+λr≥0\displaystyle c_{11}K*r(x)-K*b+\lambda_{r}\geq 0 if ​r​(x)=0,\displaystyle\quad\text{if }r(x)=0,
c22​K∗b⁡(x)−K∗r+λb≥0\displaystyle c_{22}K*b(x)-K*r+\lambda_{b}\geq 0 if ​b​(x)=0,\displaystyle\quad\text{if }b(x)=0,
c11​K∗r⁡(x)−K∗b+λr≤0\displaystyle c_{11}K*r(x)-K*b+\lambda_{r}\leq 0 if ​ρ​(x)=1,\displaystyle\quad\text{if }\rho(x)=1,
c22​K∗b⁡(x)−K∗r+λb≤0\displaystyle c_{22}K*b(x)-K*r+\lambda_{b}\leq 0 if ​ρ​(x)=1.\displaystyle\quad\text{if }\rho(x)=1.

Hence we can effectively derive conditions on the sign of the normal derivatives of

Sr=c11​K∗r−K∗b​ and ​Sb=c22​K∗b−K∗r\displaystyle S_{r}=c_{11}K*r-K*b\text{ and }S_{b}=c_{22}K*b-K*r

on interfaces between regions with r=1r=1, b=1b=1, or ρ=0\rho=0 (voids). On interfaces between red or blue and void the same analysis as in [21] applies, on interfaces between red and blue sign conditions on the derivatives of SbS_{b} and SrS_{r} need to hold simultaneously. Such stable configurations will lead to similar stationary solutions or metastable dynamics in the case of small positive ε\varepsilon.

We finally mention that for the coarsening of interfaces in the metastable case analogous laws as in [34, 21] can be derived by multiscale asymptotic expansions, whose details we leave to future research. In numerical experiments the coarsening dynamics is well observed, see Figure 8, where one obtains local unmixing followed by coarsening. In the case of small self-attraction as shown in Figure 9 a different kind of coarsening dynamics is obtained, which is not characterized by rr and bb attaining values close to 11, but a mixed phase is coarsening versus the void regions. In this case a further analysis is quite open and an interesting issue for the future.
